events.excerpt: Smartwatches are great for keeping important information within reach, but interacting with their tiny touchscreens can be a pain. And when your hands are occupied, tapping a button might not even be possible. Researchers at Northwestern University have developed an alternative that could let you control a smartwatch with simple hand and finger gestures, without ever touching its screen. Their experimental system, called EITWatch , uses electrical impedance tomography (EIT) to detect subtle changes in the muscles and tendons beneath the skin. Unlike previous systems that require specialized wristbands, EITWatch packs its sensing electrodes into an area small enough to fit on the back of a conventional smartwatch. The technology works by passing tiny alternating electrical currents through the wrist and measuring how they travel through the underlying tissues. As fingers move and muscles contract, the electrical impedance of those tissues changes. By analyzing these variations, the system can determine which gesture the wearer is making. The researchers built a prototype around a custom circuit board featuring eight gold-plated electrodes arranged in a 31-millimeter-diameter ring. These electrodes sit against the skin beneath a standard 40-millimeter watch case. The current protot
events.headline: A Smarter Way to Control Your Smartwatch

Today: Layer 2 — decisions without parties. The infrastructure problem (Layer 0) and the identity problem (Layer 1) are hard engineering challenges. Layer 2 — how we actually make decisions — is a different kind of hard. It is not an engineering problem. It is a mechanism design problem, and the failure modes are political. Every democratic system ever built has failed in at least one of the same ways: Token-weighted voting — the wealthy decide. One token, one vote is plutocracy by definition. Simple majority — ignores intensity of preference. A 51% majority with mild opinions overrides a 49% minority whose lives depend on the outcome. Representative democracy — creates permanent political classes who optimise for re-election, not for constituents. Party systems — force multidimensional human preferences into one-dimensional ideological alignments. And in all of the above: the actor with the largest megaphone wins. The best-funded campaign, the most viral narrative, the most charismatic demagogue systematically outcompetes the actor who is simply correct. "Wouldn't it be cool to drive a tiny OLED display, read a color sensor, or even just flash some LEDs directly from your computer," the company asks, rhetorically, echoing the same sentiment as when it launched the original variant of its interface board. "Sure you can program an Arduino or QT Py to talk to these devices and your computer, but why can't your computer just talk to those devices and sensors itself? Well, now your computer can talk to devices using the Adafruit MCP2222 breakout board!" The compact board is built around Microchip's MCP2222, providing a USB Type-C connector at one end and a Qwiic/STEMMA QT connector at the other — and breadboard-friendly general-purpose input/output (GPIO) pin headers along the edges between. Connected to a USB Host, it provides a way to interface with UART serial, SPI, and I2C buses, as well as its GPIO pins, with selectable 3.3V or 5V logic levels. events.excerpt: IBM has unveiled the Nighthawk r3, an upcoming next-gen quantum processor that will feature 520 qubits, as another step towards a planned fault-tolerant quantum system it hopes to launch in 2029. Big Blue's current Nighthawk r2 was only made available in September and features 120 quantum bits (qubits) capable of handling circuits using 7,500 operations. Its successor, IBM claims, will have more than four times as many qubits and execute 10,000 quantum operations to tackle larger, more complex problems while maintaining the same speed and accuracy. Nighthawk r3 is slated to arrive in 2027, when Big Blue plans to link two of the quantum processors into a single system with more than 1,000 qubits. IBM said applications increasingly require circuits executing thousands of quantum operations on approximately 100 qubits or more, speeding up collection of the millions or billions of samples needed to perform complex computations. Speed determines whether such demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost. The new quantum processor will feature 10 chip-to-chip interconnects, called l-couplers, designed for linking together processors that it will use to enable a single 1,040-qubit system. events.excerpt: At one point in the last 24 hours, Bitcoin rose to about $74,600 after shocks caused by October’s US CPI data contributed to it falling below $73,000 recently. However, at the time of writing, it was back below $73,000, with market commentary account CryptosRus suggesting that BTC has to overcome three tests for the rebound to hold. Bitcoin Rebound Faces Further Macro Pressure The first test has to do with inflation, with October’s headline Consumer Price Index rising above the anticipated 0.3% forecast to hit 0.4% month-over-month, while the core CPI increased by 0.3% against expectations of 0.2%. events.excerpt: Engineer Hao Wen is preparing a crowdfunding campaign for the Crescent City Dev Board, an Espressif ESP32-S3-based gadget with integrated 0.96" OLED display and lithium-polymer battery support — designed as a compact all-in-one for a range of use cases. "Many ESP32 projects that need a screen start as a dev board, a display module, a charger board, and jumper wires between them," Wen explains of his thinking behind the board's design. "Crescent City puts those parts on one small board. The same hardware can be a desk clock, a status display for a server or a 3D printer, or a battery-powered sensor that shows its readings on its own screen. Plug a Qwiic temperature and humidity sensor (SHT4x) into the side connector, and an example sketch shows live readings and a chart with no soldering." The board is based around an ESP32-S3-WROOM-1-N8 module, which dates from before Espressif's transition to the RISC-V architecture and features two Tensilica Xtensa LX7 cores running at up to 240MHz, 512kB of static RAM plus an additional 16kB available from the real-time clock, plus 384kB of on-chip flash storage alongside 8MB of off-chip flash. There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. events.excerpt: Encountered some odd SQL Server connection behavior since the October update? There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections. Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory. The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected. "This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time." You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems. Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. events.excerpt: Distributed AI training workloads impose complex scheduling requirements that Kubernetes’s built-in scheduler can’t meet. Kubernetes schedules pods individually and independently, but distributed training introduces two requirements that break this model: Pods must land on hardware with the right inter-GPU bandwidth, and all pods must be scheduled simultaneously. If either requirement goes unmet, training stalls or runs far below the hardware’s potential. Topology-aware scheduling (TAS) and gang scheduling address these two requirements and help organizations extract full value from GPU capacity, which represents a growing share of infrastructure spend. TAS shapes the relative placement of pods to enable fast communication between GPUs. Gang scheduling helps ensure that all pods in a distributed job start running simultaneously, preventing the partial starts that leave GPUs allocated but idle. Together, they give Kubernetes the placement precision and coordination that distributed workloads require. In this post, we’ll look at the scheduling problems that AI training presents for Kubernetes and how TAS and gang scheduling, implemented by Kueue and the Coscheduling plugin , solve them. We’ll explore: How the Kubernetes scheduler is unsuited for AI training How to validate gang sch
events.headline: Gang scheduling and topology-aware placement for AI training in Kubernetes

According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. events.excerpt: More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote. If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice. The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI. The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records.
